entities.name: Quintus Nasidius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Nasidius, often identified as Lucius Nasidius in ancient sources, was a Roman naval commander whose career spanned the tumultuous final decades of the Roman Republic in the 1st century BC. Though not a figure of paramount political authority, his strategic importance lay in his command of significant naval forces for various factions during Caesar's Civil War and its protracted aftermath. His allegiance shifts, from the senatorial optimates to Sextus Pompey and later to Mark Antony, underscore the fluid and often desperate loyalties of this era, where control of the seas was frequently decisive in determining land-based power.

Nasidius first gained prominence commanding a fleet for Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, who had established a formidable independent power base in Sicily and posed a critical threat to the Second Triumvirate's grain supply. He participated in the extensive naval campaigns against Octavian and Marcus Agrippa, culminating in the decisive Battle of Naulochus in 36 BC. Following Sextus Pompey's catastrophic defeat, Nasidius defected to Mark Antony, bringing a substantial portion of his fleet with him. He subsequently commanded a squadron for Antony in the eastern Mediterranean, notably engaging in operations off the coast of Asia Minor before joining Antony's main fleet in the lead-up to the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.
